hints: State the hypotheses using $\mu$, the population mean time for the new challenge. The old mean was $25.5$ and the claim is that students take *less* time, so $\text{H}_1$ is one-tailed.
For a sample mean, standardise with the standard error: $z = \dfrac{23.7 - 25.5}{5.2 \div \sqrt{40}}$. Note the $\sqrt{40}$, because the $23.7$ is the mean of $40$ students.
Work out $z$ to 3 decimal places. Check its sign: $23.7$ is below $25.5$, so $z$ should be negative.
A one-tailed test at 1% needs the lower-tail critical value $-2.326$. Compare your $z$ with $-2.326$ (equivalently compare its size with $2.326$).
Say whether your $z$ is in the rejection region, then write the conclusion about the mean time in context, in cautious wording ("there is evidence that" / "no evidence that"), not definite.
walkthrough:
**Hypotheses (B1)**

Let $\mu$ be the population mean time (in minutes) taken for the new challenge. We want to know whether the mean has gone *down* from $25.5$, so the test is one-tailed:

$$\text{H}_0\text{: } \mu = 25.5 \qquad \text{H}_1\text{: } \mu < 25.5$$

Why this way round? $\text{H}_0$ is the "nothing has changed" assumption. We only reject it if the sample gives strong enough evidence of a decrease.

**Distribution of the sample mean**

We are told to assume $\sigma = 5.2$. The sample has $n = 40$, which is large, so the sample mean $\bar{X}$ is approximately normal. If $\text{H}_0$ is true:

$$\bar{X} \approx \text{N}\left(25.5, \frac{5.2^2}{40}\right)$$

The standard deviation of a sample mean (the *standard error*) is $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \dfrac{5.2}{\sqrt{40}}$. It is smaller than $5.2$ because averages of $40$ students vary less than single students.

**Standardise (M1, A1)**

$$z = \frac{23.7 - 25.5}{5.2 \div \sqrt{40}}$$

This line, with the $\sqrt{40}$, earns the M1. Now step by step:

$$\sqrt{40} = 6.3245\ldots$$

$$\frac{5.2}{6.3245\ldots} = 0.8222\ldots$$

$$23.7 - 25.5 = -1.8$$

$$z = \frac{-1.8}{0.8222\ldots} = -2.1892\ldots = -2.189 \text{ (3 d.p.)}$$

This earns the A1.

**Compare with the critical value (M1)**

The test is at the $1\%$ level and one-tailed (lower tail). We need the $z$ with $1\%$ below it, which is $-2.326$ (from the table, $\Phi(2.326) = 0.99$).

The rejection region is $z < -2.326$. Our $z = -2.189$ is not that far below zero:

$$2.189 < 2.326$$

so it is **not** in the rejection region. (Equivalent: $\text{P}(Z < -2.189) = 0.0143$, which is bigger than $0.01$.)

Warning: using a two-tailed test (critical value $2.576$) caps the marks, because the question points to a decrease.

**Conclusion (A1)**

The test statistic is not in the rejection region, so we do not reject $\text{H}_0$. In context and not definite:

There is no evidence, at the $1\%$ significance level, that the mean time taken for the new challenge has decreased from $25.5$ minutes.

Avoid "the mean time is definitely $25.5$": not rejecting $\text{H}_0$ is not proof that $\text{H}_0$ is true.

**Final answer**

$z = -2.189$, which is not less than $-2.326$. Do not reject $\text{H}_0$: there is no evidence that the mean time for the new challenge is less than $25.5$ minutes.

hints: A Type I error means rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when $\text{H}_0$ is actually true. Look at your conclusion in part (a): did the test reject $\text{H}_0$?
walkthrough:
**What a Type I error is**

A Type I error happens when we **reject** $\text{H}_0$ even though $\text{H}_0$ is really true. It can only occur if the test ends in rejecting $\text{H}_0$.

In part (a) we did *not* reject $\text{H}_0$. So we could not have wrongly rejected it. (If we were wrong at all, it would be a Type II error: not rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when it is false.)

**Final answer**

No, it is not possible that a Type I error was made, because $\text{H}_0$ was not rejected in part (a).
